children: The Australian dollar drew support from strong business investment data on Thursday, a day after it whipsawed alongside global stocks in a volatile session, while the kiwi proved steadier, edging further from a 17-year low.
rose 0.2% to $0.6638, after diving to a fresh one-year low of $0.6559 on Wednesday before a rebound in global stocks helped it trim most of the losses. The currency has lost 5.6% so far in November.
The kiwi dollar was little changed at $0.5487

, after rising 0.1% in the previous session to as high as $0.5495. The gain marked a second straight day of advances, snapping a 10-day losing streak and helping the currency avoid a break below its 17-year low of $0.5434.

Data on Thursday showed Australian business investment surged anew in the September quarter as firms poured money into data centres, recording its biggest rise since 2011 at the height of the mining boom. Much of the spending went on imported equipment, however, which offsets its boost to economic growth. Businesses also further upgraded their investment plans for the near future.

Harry McAuley, economist for Oxford Economics Australia, said he expects investment in data centres to grow from A$20 billion ($13 billion) this year to about A$60 billion by 2030, but that it is likely to be lumpy between quarters.

"Leading indicators show plenty of new projects breaking ground, while policy support and demand-side drivers all point towards strength in the near term. As such we expect investment to remain the engine room of the economy through 2027," he said.
Markets are still wagering that the next move in interest rates will be down, but do not fully price a first cut until August. They now see an 83% chance of a June cut.

After the data, Australia's 3-year government bond futures (YTTc1) gave up gains to trade flat at 95.54, having hit a five-month high of 95.61 earlier in the day. They have rallied for six consecutive sessions on rate cut expectations despite the hot inflation print on Wednesday.

Across the Tasman Sea, swaps now imply an 80% probability that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand will raise interest rates by a quarter percentage point to 3%, with 75 basis points of tightening priced in by the end of next year. (0#NZDIRPR)
, after losing 0.3% on Wednesday to hit the lowest level since late August. It is down nearly 4% from its 13-year peak of NZ$1.2601 in October.
